scenes.tts: In chapter 1, the microtubules placed the band, and the cut fell between the two sets of chromosomes. But the cut splits everything else too. Does the cell count its organelles out, or is chance good enough?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD continues from chapter 1 (16:9, dark background), same colour map: microtubules of the spindle and asters BLUE; membrane and cortex a thick GREY rim; active RhoA AMBER; the actin and myosin ring MAGENTA; chromosomes WHITE. NEW for chapter 2, fixed for the rest of the film: small organelle units (generic copies) TEAL dots; the later Golgi example VIOLET; the later mitochondrial example LIME GREEN; centrosomes small bright BLUE squares at the centre of each aster. Open on chapter 1's round sea urchin embryo cell, filling about 75% of frame height, in anaphase: white chromosome clusters drifting apart, blue spindle and asters flickering, the amber stripe at the equator and a magenta ring starting to tighten. On 'in chapter 1', a small corner tag 'Chapter 1' glows and fades. On 'splits everything else', about thirty generic teal organelle units fade in through the cytoplasm and drift slowly. Do not add a Golgi ribbon or mitochondrial network to this sea urchin cell; those later pictures are mammalian cell-line examples. A dashed white line sweeps down through the equator, cutting across the teal units. On 'count its organelles', a white question card fades in at the top: 'Count them out, or leave it to chance?' Label at top left, size 30, white: 'what lands on each side?'
scenes.narration: In chapter 1, the microtubules placed the band, and the cut fell between the two sets of chromosomes. But the cut splits everything else too. Does the cell count its organelles out, or is chance good enough?

scenes.visual: Title 'Chance or Control' fades in across the lower third for 2 s while the teal dots keep drifting and the magenta ring keeps tightening slowly; the question card stays at the top.

scenes.tts: Start with the simplest model: no control at all. Each copy of an organelle goes to either daughter by a coin toss, on its own.
scenes.visual: The cell finishes dividing into two rounded daughters side by side, left and right, joined by a thin grey bridge as at the end of chapter 1. Show, then tell: one teal dot near the old equator lifts out, a small white coin spins beside it, lands, and the dot glides into the left daughter. A second dot: coin spins, lands, dot glides right. Then several more in quick succession, each with its own coin, each choosing independently. Label above the daughters, size 30, white: 'each copy: a coin toss'. Small key bottom right, teal dot 'one copy' (size 28), stays for the film.
scenes.narration: Start with the simplest model: no control at all. Each copy of an organelle goes to either daughter by a coin toss, on its own.

scenes.visual: Show, then tell: the coins keep spinning over the bridge and teal dots keep gliding left or right one at a time, about ten more, with no pattern; the two daughters slowly fill. A small tally above each daughter ticks up unevenly.

scenes.tts: With a hundred copies, the count in one daughter averages fifty, give or take about five. Most daughters get forty to sixty. The chance that either daughter gets none is about one point six times ten to the minus thirty. In practice, that never happens.
scenes.caption: With a hundred copies, the count in one daughter averages fifty, give or take about five. Most daughters get forty to sixty. The chance that either daughter gets none is about 1.6 × 10^-30. In practice, that never happens.
scenes.visual: Fill both daughters with teal dots shared by fast coin tosses, 100 in all (tiny coins flicker over the bridge). A counter above each daughter ticks up, size 34, white, landing near 50 each (for example 47 and 53). On 'give or take', a COMPUTED histogram slides in along the bottom third: the binomial distribution for n = 100, p = 0.5, x axis 'copies in left daughter' 30 to 70, bars teal, the bars from 40 to 60 brighter with a bracket labelled '40 to 60: most divisions'. Beside the histogram, show the separate computed statement 'either daughter empty: 2 × 0.5^100 = 1.6 × 10^-30', size 28. Do not attach that two-daughter probability to the histogram's x = 0 endpoint, which would represent only the left daughter being empty. Corner label 'computed'.
scenes.narration: With a hundred copies, the count in one daughter averages fifty, give or take about five. Most daughters get forty to sixty. The chance that either daughter gets none is about 1.6 × 10^-30. In practice, that never happens.

scenes.visual: The computed histogram settles; its brighter 40-to-60 bars pulse once, and the separate statement 'either daughter empty: 2 × 0.5^100 = 1.6 × 10^-30' stays visible. The counters above the daughters hold.

scenes.tts: Now shrink the stock to just two copies, tossed the same way. How often does one daughter end up with none?
scenes.visual: The 100 teal dots and the histogram wipe away. A fresh pair of daughters, still joined by the bridge, holds nothing. Exactly two teal dots sit at the old equator, each with a coin hovering above it, ready to spin but not spinning. On 'How often', a white question card fades in at the top: 'Two copies: how often is one daughter empty?'
scenes.narration: Now shrink the stock to just two copies, tossed the same way. How often does one daughter end up with none?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. The question card stays on screen. The two coins wobble on their edges without falling; the daughters breathe gently and the bridge pulses faintly so the frame is not frozen.

scenes.tts: Half the time. Both copies can land left, or both right; each happens one time in four. Either daughter can be the empty one, so together they make one in two.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. A 2 by 2 grid of four small daughter pairs builds on screen, one per outcome, each labelled with its coins: 'left, left', 'left, right', 'right, left', 'right, right'. In each pair the two teal dots sit where the coins sent them. On 'both can land left', the 'left, left' pair glows and its empty right daughter flashes white; on 'both can land right', the 'right, right' pair does the same for its left daughter. Under each glowing pair, '1 in 4' (size 30). On 'together they make one in two', the two glowing pairs slide together and a label '1 in 4 + 1 in 4 = 1 in 2' appears, size 34, white.
scenes.narration: Half the time. Both copies can land left, or both right; each happens one time in four. Either daughter can be the empty one, so together they make one in two.

scenes.tts: The chance of an empty daughter is two times one half to the power n. Each added copy halves the risk. At ten copies it is about one in five hundred. At twenty-one copies it drops below one in a million.
scenes.caption: The chance of an empty daughter is 2 × 0.5^n. Each added copy halves the risk. At ten copies it is about one in five hundred. At twenty-one copies it drops below one in a million.
scenes.visual: The grid shrinks into the top left corner. A COMPUTED graph fills the centre: x axis 'number of copies, n' from 1 to 25, y axis 'chance one daughter gets none' on a log scale from 1 down to 0.0000001, with the equation shown above it, size 34: 'P(empty) = 2 × 0.5^n'. A teal line draws itself left to right in time with the words, starting at the point n = 2, P = 0.5 (a dot labelled '2 copies: 1 in 2'). On 'halves the risk', small steps of the line flash one by one. On 'ten copies', a dot at n = 10 labelled 'about 1 in 500' (0.2%). On 'twenty-one copies', a dashed horizontal line labelled '1 in a million' appears and the line crosses below it at n = 21, marked with a dot. Corner label 'computed'.
scenes.narration: The chance of an empty daughter is 2 × 0.5^n. Each added copy halves the risk. At ten copies it is about one in five hundred. At twenty-one copies it drops below one in a million.

scenes.visual: The teal curve finishes drawing to n = 25 and keeps falling below the dashed one-in-a-million line; the three labelled dots (2, 10, 21) pulse once each, left to right.

scenes.tts: So chance is safe only for many independent units. But some organelles are one connected structure, like a mammalian cell's Golgi ribbon, or a tubular mitochondrial network. To the coin, each is a single copy.
scenes.visual: The graph slides down to a thin strip along the bottom. Transition from the sea urchin and coin-toss views to a generic schematic mammalian cell entering mitosis, labelled 'mammalian examples', with teal dots scattered. On 'safe only for many', the teal dots twinkle. On 'Golgi ribbon', a violet long folded band appears and is labelled 'Golgi ribbon' (violet, size 30). On 'tubular network', a lime tubular network appears and is labelled 'mitochondrial network' (lime, size 30). On 'a single copy', one white coin hovers over the whole violet ribbon and one over the whole lime network, and the strip graph's point at n = 1 glows: 'n = 1: always one empty daughter'. Label at top, size 30, white: 'connected = one unit'.
scenes.narration: So chance is safe only for many independent units. But some organelles are one connected structure, like a mammalian cell's Golgi ribbon, or a tubular mitochondrial network. To the coin, each is a single copy.

scenes.visual: Show, then tell: the violet Golgi ribbon begins to shimmer and its folds loosen, the first small violet fragments starting to pull away from the band. Already-condensed chromosomes and the forming spindle remain in the background; do not show them condensing inside an intact nucleus. Nothing is labelled yet.

scenes.tts: Such a structure must be broken up first, or moved actively. In PtK1 cells, a rat-kangaroo kidney line, the Golgi ribbon comes apart during mitosis. Its membranes cluster around the spindle poles. After division, the ribbon reforms.
scenes.visual: Label at top left, size 30, white: 'PtK1 cells (rat-kangaroo)'. Show, then tell: the violet ribbon breaks into many small violet fragments, which drift toward the two blue asters and gather in two loose clouds around the spindle poles, labelled 'clustered at the poles' (violet, size 28). The furrow closes and the cell becomes two daughters; in each daughter the violet fragments slide together and fuse back into a shorter folded ribbon, labelled 'ribbon reforms'. Schematic: corner label 'schematic'. Do not show any Golgi membranes riding on the spindle itself or entering the bridge.
scenes.narration: Such a structure must be broken up first, or moved actively. In PtK1 cells, a rat-kangaroo kidney line, the Golgi ribbon comes apart during mitosis. Its membranes cluster around the spindle poles. After division, the ribbon reforms.

scenes.tts: Mitochondria in HeLa cells, a human cell line, broke into fragments early in mitosis. Without Drp1, a protein that drives mitochondrial fission, they stayed tubular. That is one cell line, so treat it as a strong lead.
scenes.visual: Label at top left changes to 'HeLa cells (human)'. Split frame, two copies of the same undivided cell entering mitosis. Left, labelled 'normal': the lime tubular network snaps into many short lime pieces, which scatter through the cytoplasm. Right, labelled 'no Drp1': the lime network stays long and tubular as the cell rounds up. A small labelled block 'Drp1' (lime outline, no structure) pinches a tube once on the left side to show what it does, then the label 'fission' appears beside it. On 'one cell line', a white tag 'one cell line: a strong lead' appears under the split. Corner label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Mitochondria in HeLa cells, a human cell line, broke into fragments early in mitosis. Without Drp1, a protein that drives mitochondrial fission, they stayed tubular. That is one cell line, so treat it as a strong lead.

scenes.visual: The split frame holds: left, short lime fragments drifting; right, the long lime tubes swaying gently. The tag 'one cell line: a strong lead' stays.

scenes.tts: Some things are not left to chance. The two centrosomes sit at the spindle poles, and the spindle carries one to each pole. So microtubules return: they place the cut, and carry part of the inheritance.
scenes.visual: Back to the single sea urchin cell in anaphase, the split frame gone. The two small blue centrosome squares at the centres of the asters brighten, labelled 'centrosome' (blue, size 30). As the chromosomes separate, each centrosome rides outward with its pole, one to each side, with no coin anywhere near them. On 'microtubules return', the amber stripe at the equator re-lights and a short strip builds across the bottom, two labelled blocks with arrows: blue 'microtubules' to amber 'place the cut', and blue 'microtubules' to blue 'carry centrosomes'.
scenes.narration: Some things are not left to chance. The two centrosomes sit at the spindle poles, and the spindle carries one to each pole. So microtubules return: they place the cut, and carry part of the inheritance.

scenes.tts: One caution. Moving an organelle is not the same as changing its share. Each claim needs its own test.
scenes.visual: Lime mitochondria in the dividing cell drift toward the furrow, with a small label 'moved'. Beside it, a balance scale (white, simple line drawing) with a lime pile on each pan stays level, labelled 'shares?' with a white question mark. The two labels sit apart, separated by a thin white line, to show they are separate claims. Nothing on screen says which way the scale tips.
scenes.narration: One caution. Moving an organelle is not the same as changing its share. Each claim needs its own test.

scenes.visual: Show, then tell. A generic schematic summary cell completes its division: the magenta ring tightens, and the two daughters part to a thin bridge. A corner label reads 'examples from different cells'. Inside each: a crowd of teal dots shared by chance, a reformed violet ribbon, lime fragments, and one blue centrosome. Do not present this composite as the sea urchin, PtK1 or HeLa experiment itself. No narration; the motion is the point.

scenes.tts: So the cell need not count every unit. Chance can share many small units, often with some control alongside. Chance is safe only for many units; one connected unit needs control.
scenes.visual: Hold on the schematic summary daughters and keep the label 'examples from different cells'. On 'Chance can share many small units', a white coin flickers once over the teal dots in each daughter. On 'some control alongside', a faint blue glow passes over the centrosomes. On 'one connected unit', the violet ribbon in each daughter pulses, and a brief replay in miniature shows a ribbon breaking into fragments and reforming. The strip graph from earlier re-lights its teal curve for a moment.
scenes.narration: So the cell need not count every unit. Chance can share many small units, often with some control alongside. Chance is safe only for many units; one connected unit needs control.

scenes.line: Chance is safe only for many units; one connected unit needs control.
scenes.visual: End card over the two daughters (dimmed to 30%): the take-home line, size 40, white with 'many units' in teal and 'connected unit' in violet: 'Chance is safe only for many units; one connected unit needs control.' The bridge pulses gently.
